bibl.title: River plastic emissions to the world’s oceans

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: the mass of plastic entering the ocean from rivers each year, and how it is distributed in space and across the seasons
span.quote: We estimate that between 1.15 and 2.41 million tonnes of plastic waste currently enters the ocean every year from rivers, with over 74% of emissions occurring between May and October. The top 20 polluting rivers, mostly located in Asia, account for 67% of the global total.

span.label: how much plastic inland populations contribute to the ocean through rivers - a global figure that did not exist, where the coastal contribution already did
span.quote: While a quantification of land-based inputs from coastal populations (<50 km from coastline) worldwide already exists, no global assessment of contributions from inland populations through riverine systems has been proposed to date.

span.label: a global model of riverine plastic input calibrated against 30 field observations from 13 rivers, giving 1.15-2.41 million tonnes per year with its seasonality and its top contributors named
span.quote: We estimate that between 1.15 and 2.41 million tonnes of plastic waste currently enters the ocean every year from rivers, with over 74% of emissions occurring between May and October. The top 20 polluting rivers, mostly located in Asia, account for 67% of the global total.

span.label: existence
span.quote: We estimate that between 1.15 and 2.41 million tonnes of plastic waste currently enters the ocean every year from rivers, with over 74% of emissions occurring between May and October. The top 20 polluting rivers, mostly located in Asia, account for 67% of the global total.

span.label: a global flux nobody had measured, whose magnitude turns out to be set by waste management and monsoon rainfall in a handful of Asian catchments
span.quote: We estimated that >74.5% of the total river plastic input occurs between May and October. Our model showed a peak in global inputs for the month of August with an estimated 228,800 (range 193,000–375,000) tonnes, and a low for the month of January with 46,200 (range 34,200–87,500) tonnes. These seasonal findings were mainly driven by the large inputs from China which are regulated by the East Asian monsoon.

span.label: an empirical model of mismanaged plastic waste times catchment runoff, fitted to surface-water observations and propagated over 40,760 watersheds, with dams treated as sinks
span.term: an empirical model of mismanaged plastic waste times catchment runoff, fitted to surface-water observations and propagated over 40,760 watersheds, with dams treated as sinks
span.quote: River plastic mass concentrations from the literature (Table 3) demonstrated a statistically significant, positive correlation with the product of annual MPW production rates inside a catchment area downstream of artificial barriers and monthly averaged catchment runoff (Pearson product-moment test, r=0.4132, P<0.05, n=29). The correlation test was conducted after removing measurement data from the Yangtze River, considered as an outlier. When including data from the Yangtze River, we logically obtained a much higher, yet biased correlation (r=0.99, P<0.05, n=30).

span.label: mismanaged waste sits on land until rainfall mobilises it; surface runoff both introduces new plastic to the river during heavy rain and remobilises deposited particles during floods, so input tracks the monsoon rather than the population
span.quote: We estimated that >74.5% of the total river plastic input occurs between May and October. Our model showed a peak in global inputs for the month of August with an estimated 228,800 (range 193,000–375,000) tonnes, and a low for the month of January with 46,200 (range 34,200–87,500) tonnes. These seasonal findings were mainly driven by the large inputs from China which are regulated by the East Asian monsoon.

span.label: an artificial barrier intercepts surface plastic, so the load reaching the river mouth reflects only the catchment area downstream of the last dam - which is why moving that boundary changes the global total
span.quote: Artificial barriers in rivers may retain 65% of the global input into freshwater, as we calculated an annual 2.13–4.46 million tonnes of plastic introduced upstream of dams that are not accounted as input into the oceans by our model.

span.label: one catchment with plastic concentrations orders of magnitude above every other sampled river dominates a regression across 30 points, so including it raises the correlation from 0.41 to 0.99 without the model having improved
span.term: outlier leverage on a fitted correlation
span.quote: River plastic mass concentrations from the literature (Table 3) demonstrated a statistically significant, positive correlation with the product of annual MPW production rates inside a catchment area downstream of artificial barriers and monthly averaged catchment runoff (Pearson product-moment test, r=0.4132, P<0.05, n=29). The correlation test was conducted after removing measurement data from the Yangtze River, considered as an outlier. When including data from the Yangtze River, we logically obtained a much higher, yet biased correlation (r=0.99, P<0.05, n=30).

span.label: the model rests on the assumption that dams intercept ALL plastic, which the authors name as a major assumption; 2.13-4.46 million tonnes per year is generated upstream of dams and simply not counted
span.quote: Furthermore, a major assumption of our model is that artificial barriers such as dams act as sinks for all plastic particles. This is a conservative assumption since sediment trap efficiency of reservoirs may vary upon several factors.

span.label: there is very little data to document the assumptions about Asian contributions or to thoroughly verify the validity of the model - stated by the authors about the region that supplies 86% of their total
span.quote: Research on freshwater plastic pollution is a relatively new field and most efforts have been carried out in industrialized countries of Europe and North America. While many indicators suggest a dominant contribution of plastics from Asian countries, there is very little data to document these assumptions and thoroughly verify the validity of our model.

span.label: the estimate covers only the sampled size spectrum - nothing below the net mesh, nothing above the trawl aperture, nothing below the sampled depth - so it is conservative by construction
span.quote: The studies used for this assessment report only a fraction of the wide plastic debris size spectrum: from particles larger than their net mesh sizes (typically 0.3 mm) to objects smaller than the aperture size of their sampling devices (typically 0.5 m). Therefore, our global river plastic input estimate is conservative, as we neglect the contribution of debris outside the sampled size range and below the surface sampling devices.

span.label: the global prediction doubles from the lower to the upper estimate once the extrapolation uncertainties in the calibration dataset are propagated
span.quote: For instance, when taking into account the uncertainties related to the extrapolations we made in the field observation dataset, our global input prediction doubled from lower to upper estimates (Supplementary Table 1).

span.label: studies reporting only particle counts were converted to mass using a mean micro/macro ratio and mean particle masses measured AT SEA, not in rivers - an extrapolation the authors name as a limitation of the calibration
span.quote: We acknowledge however, that the extrapolations described above are a limitation of the calibration exercise presented here, as the average mass of river plastic particles, as well as the ratio between micro- and macro-plastic concentrations may vary across catchments due to local differences in in-situ fragmentation rates, plastic transport processes and levels of primary micro-plastic emissions

span.label: the hydrological model's discharge predictions are known to run dryer than observations across 66 basins, attributed to precipitation uncertainty
span.quote: Nonetheless, it is important to notice that comparisons between river discharge predictions from GLDAS and observations in 66 basins worldwide demonstrated that predictions are somewhat dryer than observations. The authors of this validation study attributed the differences to uncertainties in precipitation rates.

span.label: observed plastic concentrations differ by several orders of magnitude between sampled rivers, and sampling designs, devices and reported units vary substantially - so the calibration set is heterogeneous before any model is fitted
span.quote: Sampling design and devices, as well as reported units (for example, pieces per m2, grams per m3) vary substantially between different assessments.

span.label: land-surface hydrology - the GLDAS/NOAH runoff model built for terrestrial water and energy budgets - carried into a plastic-transport estimate as the seasonality term
span.quote: Nonetheless, it is important to notice that comparisons between river discharge predictions from GLDAS and observations in 66 basins worldwide demonstrated that predictions are somewhat dryer than observations. The authors of this validation study attributed the differences to uncertainties in precipitation rates.

span.label: mean particle masses and the micro-to-macro ratio measured in the open ocean, carried into rivers to convert particle counts into mass where studies reported only counts
span.quote: Not all studies considered here reported micro- and macro-plastic concentrations at surface waters of rivers. As such, for our midpoint estimate, we homogenized our data set using the mean ratio micro- to macro-plastic numerical concentration from studies reporting both types (mean ratio equals to 0.04). For comparison, a study compiling thousands of samples at sea found a relatively similar mean ratio of 0.07 (ref.).

span.label: removing the Yangtze measurement as an outlier before testing the model-observation correlation, rather than reporting the flattering fit
span.note: eliminates: a model-observation correlation carried by one extreme measurement · outcome: held
span.quote: River plastic mass concentrations from the literature (Table 3) demonstrated a statistically significant, positive correlation with the product of annual MPW production rates inside a catchment area downstream of artificial barriers and monthly averaged catchment runoff (Pearson product-moment test, r=0.4132, P<0.05, n=29). The correlation test was conducted after removing measurement data from the Yangtze River, considered as an outlier. When including data from the Yangtze River, we logically obtained a much higher, yet biased correlation (r=0.99, P<0.05, n=30).

span.label: re-deriving the regression with mismanaged waste counted upstream of dams as well, to test whether the global answer depends on where a dam is treated as a sink
span.note: eliminates: a global input figure that depends on whether a dam is treated as a sink · outcome: partial
span.quote: While determining regression coefficients based on MPW quantities upstream of dams, our model predicted a global input of 0.76–1.55 million tonnes per year (midpoint at 0.91 million tonnes per year) which remains in the same order of magnitude than the initial scenario.

span.label: choosing monthly rather than yearly averaged runoff, tested against the observed flux inputs instead of assumed
span.note: eliminates: a runoff averaging window chosen because it fits, rather than because it predicts the observed flux · outcome: held
span.quote: A better correlation was found with estimated flux inputs from observational studies when considering monthly averaged runoff instead of the yearly average (Table 4).

span.label: a sensitivity analysis over the micro/macro ratio and mean particle masses, using the ranges observed at sea
span.note: eliminates: a mass estimate that holds only at one assumed micro-to-macro ratio and one assumed particle mass · outcome: partial
span.quote: A sensitivity analysis was conducted by varying the mean ratio micro- to macro-plastic numerical concentration (range: 0.01–0.12) and the average mass of particles (range: 0.002–0.004 g and 0.04–0.33 g for micro- and macro-plastic, respectively) using range values found at sea.

span.label: applying the same model to coastal populations, so the new estimate could be placed against the existing coastal one on its own terms
span.note: eliminates: a river estimate and a coastal estimate that cannot be compared because they were produced by different models · outcome: held
span.quote: Nonetheless, for comparison purposes, we applied our model to calculate the contribution of coastal populations (that is, living within 50 km from the coastline) and obtained a global contribution from coastal population of 356,000–893,000 tonnes per year. This suggests that at least 2.8–18.6% of the coastal plastic emissions occur via river transport. Furthermore, our findings indicate that an additional plastic input of at least 0.79–1.52 million tonnes per year reaches oceans from inland areas via rivers.

span.label: the hydrological model's discharge predictions checked against observations in 66 basins worldwide
span.note: eliminates: a plastic flux resting on modelled discharge that was never checked against a gauge · outcome: partial
span.quote: Nonetheless, it is important to notice that comparisons between river discharge predictions from GLDAS and observations in 66 basins worldwide demonstrated that predictions are somewhat dryer than observations. The authors of this validation study attributed the differences to uncertainties in precipitation rates.

span.label: mass balance
span.quote: The findings of this study provide baseline data for ocean plastic mass balance exercises, and assist in prioritizing future plastic debris monitoring and mitigation strategies.

span.label: MPW
span.quote: The consideration of dams in our numerical model was motivated by a better correlation found with measurements (Table 4) than when including MPW production rates upstream of dams.

span.label: artificial barriers
span.quote: Furthermore, a major assumption of our model is that artificial barriers such as dams act as sinks for all plastic particles. This is a conservative assumption since sediment trap efficiency of reservoirs may vary upon several factors.

span.label: catchment runoff
span.quote: A better correlation was found with estimated flux inputs from observational studies when considering monthly averaged runoff instead of the yearly average (Table 4). Therefore, monthly averaged catchment runoff corresponding to sampling event month was considered while calibrating our

span.label: buoyant plastics
span.quote: It is also important to note that our model is calibrated against buoyant plastics found on river surface waters, whereas this previous coastal contribution assessment considers all types of plastics found in municipal waste.

span.label: macro-plastic
span.quote: Not all studies considered here reported micro- and macro-plastic concentrations at surface waters of rivers. As such, for our midpoint estimate, we homogenized our data set using the mean ratio micro- to macro-plastic numerical concentration from studies reporting both types (mean ratio equals to 0.04). For comparison, a study compiling thousands of samples at sea found a relatively similar mean ratio of 0.07 (ref.).

span.label: Yangtze River
span.quote: River plastic mass concentrations from the literature (Table 3) demonstrated a statistically significant, positive correlation with the product of annual MPW production rates inside a catchment area downstream of artificial barriers and monthly averaged catchment runoff (Pearson product-moment test, r=0.4132, P<0.05, n=29). The correlation test was conducted after removing measurement data from the Yangtze River, considered as an outlier. When including data from the Yangtze River, we logically obtained a much higher, yet biased correlation (r=0.99, P<0.05, n=30).

span.label: coastal populations
span.quote: It has been estimated that between 4.8 and 12.7 million tonnes of plastic enters the ocean every year from coastal populations worldwide. Plastics within coastal areas however do not only enter the oceans through rivers. It can also reach oceans by other processes such as direct littering near beaches, followed by tidal or wind transport.

span.label: sensitivity analysis
span.quote: A sensitivity analysis was conducted by varying the mean ratio micro- to macro-plastic numerical concentration (range: 0.01–0.12) and the average mass of particles (range: 0.002–0.004 g and 0.04–0.33 g for micro- and macro-plastic, respectively) using range values found at sea.

span.label: monthly averaged runoff

span.label: model-observation correlation - WITH THE YANGTZE EXCLUDED as an outlier: r=0.4132, P<0.05, n=29. The value the paper uses
span.quote: River plastic mass concentrations from the literature (Table 3) demonstrated a statistically significant, positive correlation with the product of annual MPW production rates inside a catchment area downstream of artificial barriers and monthly averaged catchment runoff (Pearson product-moment test, r=0.4132, P<0.05, n=29). The correlation test was conducted after removing measurement data from the Yangtze River, considered as an outlier. When including data from the Yangtze River, we logically obtained a much higher, yet biased correlation (r=0.99, P<0.05, n=30).

span.label: model-observation correlation - WITH THE YANGTZE INCLUDED: r=0.99, P<0.05, n=30, which the authors call much higher and biased. One data point separates the two
span.quote: River plastic mass concentrations from the literature (Table 3) demonstrated a statistically significant, positive correlation with the product of annual MPW production rates inside a catchment area downstream of artificial barriers and monthly averaged catchment runoff (Pearson product-moment test, r=0.4132, P<0.05, n=29). The correlation test was conducted after removing measurement data from the Yangtze River, considered as an outlier. When including data from the Yangtze River, we logically obtained a much higher, yet biased correlation (r=0.99, P<0.05, n=30).

span.label: global river plastic input - COUNTING MISMANAGED WASTE DOWNSTREAM OF DAMS: 1.15-2.41 million tonnes per year. The published headline
span.quote: We estimate that between 1.15 and 2.41 million tonnes of plastic waste currently enters the ocean every year from rivers, with over 74% of emissions occurring between May and October. The top 20 polluting rivers, mostly located in Asia, account for 67% of the global total.

span.label: global river plastic input - COUNTING WASTE UPSTREAM OF DAMS TOO: 0.76-1.55 million tonnes per year, midpoint 0.91. Same model, same data, a different decision about where a dam stops being a sink
span.quote: While determining regression coefficients based on MPW quantities upstream of dams, our model predicted a global input of 0.76–1.55 million tonnes per year (midpoint at 0.91 million tonnes per year) which remains in the same order of magnitude than the initial scenario.

span.label: extends → the global estimate of plastic entering the ocean from coastal populations (4.8-12.7 million tonnes per year), by adding the inland contribution transported by rivers
span.quote: It has been estimated that between 4.8 and 12.7 million tonnes of plastic enters the ocean every year from coastal populations worldwide. Plastics within coastal areas however do not only enter the oceans through rivers. It can also reach oceans by other processes such as direct littering near beaches, followed by tidal or wind transport.

span.label: qualifies → direct comparison between riverine and coastal plastic input estimates, which measure different materials by different methods
span.quote: It is also important to note that our model is calibrated against buoyant plastics found on river surface waters, whereas this previous coastal contribution assessment considers all types of plastics found in municipal waste.

span.label: critiques → the state of freshwater plastic monitoring - unstandardised methodologies, incompatible reported units, and particle counts published without masses
span.quote: Methodologies and reported units should be better standardized, as these vary widely across assessments. Furthermore, plastics should not be regarded as a generic material but must be classified into classes (for example, polymer types, debris sizes).

span.label: builds-on → the local river sampling studies from Europe, Asia and the Americas that supply the 30 calibration observations across 13 rivers
span.quote: Overall, observed plastic concentrations differ by several orders of magnitude in between sampled rivers, with studies suggesting that population density, levels of urbanization and industrialization within catchment areas, rainfall rates and the presence of artificial barriers such as weirs and dams play a significant role in resulting rates of river-based plastic inputs into the ocean.

span.label: monthly averaged runoff —contrasted-with→ catchment runoff
span.note: differs in: the averaging window of the runoff term · the relation itself is separately evidenced · strength of the relation: 0.85
span.quote: A better correlation was found with estimated flux inputs from observational studies when considering monthly averaged runoff instead of the yearly average (Table 4).

span.label: buoyant plastics —contrasted-with→ coastal populations

span.quote: It is also important to note that our model is calibrated against buoyant plastics found on river surface waters, whereas this previous coastal contribution assessment considers all types of plastics found in municipal waste.

span.quote: The findings of this study provide baseline data for ocean plastic mass balance exercises, and assist in prioritizing future plastic debris monitoring and mitigation strategies.

span.quote: Furthermore, a major assumption of our model is that artificial barriers such as dams act as sinks for all plastic particles. This is a conservative assumption since sediment trap efficiency of reservoirs may vary upon several factors.

Plastics within coastal areas however do not only enter the oceans through rivers. It can also reach oceans by other processes such as direct littering near beaches, followed by tidal or wind transport.

span.label: share of the global total from the top 20 polluting rivers
span.quote: We estimate that between 1.15 and 2.41 million tonnes of plastic waste currently enters the ocean every year from rivers, with over 74% of emissions occurring between May and October. The top 20 polluting rivers, mostly located in Asia, account for 67% of the global total.

span.label: share of the global total from Asian rivers
span.quote: Estimated plastic releases from Asian rivers represented 86% of the total global input. A considerably high-population density combined with relatively large MPW production rates and episodes of heavy rainfalls, resulted in this dominant contribution from the Asian continent, with an estimated annual input of 1.21 (range 1.00–2.06) million tonnes per year.

span.label: share of freshwater plastic input the model treats as retained behind dams
span.quote: Artificial barriers in rivers may retain 65% of the global input into freshwater, as we calculated an annual 2.13–4.46 million tonnes of plastic introduced upstream of dams that are not accounted as input into the oceans by our model.
